--- format: revealjs title: Distances title-slide-attributes: data-notes: | How do we calculate the similarity between examples? One way to calculate the similarity between two points in high dimensional space is by calculating the distance between them. So, if the distance is higher, that means that the points are less similar and when the distance is smaller, that means that the points are more similar. --- ## Distance between vectors **Euclidean distance**: Euclidean distance is a measure of the true straight line distance between two points in Euclidean space. Subtract the two cities: ::: {#745db02e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} two_cities.iloc[1] - two_cities.iloc[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` longitude -13.2789 latitude -1.7199 dtype: float64 ``` ::: :::
Square the differences: ::: {#9e4a5055 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} (two_cities.iloc[1] - two_cities.iloc[0])**2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` longitude 176.329185 latitude 2.958056 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: :::{.notes} How do we calculate the distance between these two points (two cities)? Let's calculate the Euclidean distance between these two cities so here are our two cities. The first step is to subtract these two cities. We are subtracting the city at index 0 from the city at index 1. Next, we square the differences. ::: --- Sum them up: ::: {#c0837290 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} ((two_cities.iloc[1] - two_cities.iloc[0])**2).sum() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` np.float64(179.28724121999983) ``` ::: :::
And then take the square root: ::: {#3f1bc058 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} np.sqrt(np.sum((two_cities.iloc[1] - two_cities.iloc[0])**2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` np.float64(13.389818565611703) ``` ::: ::: :::{.notes} Our third step is summing up the squared differences. Then finally we take the square root of the value. This results in a value of 13.3898 which is the distance between the two cities. ::: --- ::: {#e2dcef10 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} np.sqrt(np.sum((two_cities.iloc[1] - two_cities.iloc[0])**2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` np.float64(13.389818565611703) ``` ::: :::
::: {#dfa88ca3 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import euclidean_distances euclidean_distances(two_cities) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` array([[ 0. , 13.38981857], [13.38981857, 0. ]]) ``` ::: ::: :::{.notes} `sklearn` has a function called `euclidean_distances` that we could use instead of going through each of the steps on the previous slide. When we call this function on our two cities data, it outputs this matrix with four values. - Our first value is the distance between city 0 and itself. - Our second value is the distance between city 0 and city1. - Our third value is the distance between city 1and city 0. - Our fourth value is the distance between city 1 and itself. As we can see, the distances are symmetric. If we calculate the distance between city 0 and city, it’s going to have the same value as if we calculated the distance between city 1 and city 0. This isn’t always the case if we use a different metric to calculate distances. ::: # Let’s apply what we learned!
